questions.question: Which tier should retain authority for an immediate machine safety action during a cloud partition?
options: The cloud because it has the largest model
The device or site-local safety controller with a bounded fallback
Whichever tier most recently wrote a timestamp
The telemetry backend
questions.explanation: A remote control plane cannot own an immediate safety action when its availability is outside the deadline. Local safety authority and a tested degraded path must remain explicit.

questions.question: A node advertises enough accelerator capacity but only 5% memory headroom after loading the model. What should admission do?
options: Admit because accelerator capacity is the only relevant signal
Admit and disable telemetry
Reject or reschedule because memory pressure can break runtime stability
Move the device clock forward
questions.explanation: Admission evaluates the complete resource contract. Accelerator presence does not compensate for insufficient memory headroom.

questions.question: Why is a valid artifact signature insufficient by itself?
options: Signatures make models slower
Authenticity does not prove runtime compatibility, input schema compatibility, freshness, or task quality
Signed artifacts cannot be cached
Signatures replace digests
questions.explanation: Signature verification establishes artifact identity under a trust policy. Separate gates must validate digest binding, freshness, runtime and model contracts, and observed outcomes.

questions.question: What is the safest behavior when an edge site is offline but still inside its signed offline lease?
options: Promote a new fleet model locally
Continue the approved current model, buffer bounded observations, and expire stale commands
Accept every cached command regardless of age
Overwrite the device safety state from the last cloud snapshot
questions.explanation: An offline lease can permit bounded continuation, not independent promotion of fleet intent. Events need stable IDs and commands need expiry.

questions.question: Why is wall-clock last-write-wins a weak reconnect policy for an edge fleet?
options: It uses too little storage
Clock order does not encode field authority and can overwrite safety state or replay stale intent
It prevents any device telemetry
It requires model quantization
questions.explanation: Reconciliation needs explicit owners, monotonic versions or sequence numbers, idempotent event IDs, and command expiry. A timestamp alone cannot express those semantics.

questions.question: A canary has healthy CPU and memory but task drift exceeds the ring budget. What is the correct rollout decision?
options: Promote because infrastructure is healthy
Increase telemetry cardinality until the alert disappears
Contain or roll back the canary and investigate task evidence
Delete the previous model
questions.explanation: Model behavior can fail while infrastructure remains healthy. Promotion must include task outcomes and drift evidence.

questions.question: Which telemetry attribute is most likely to create a privacy and cardinality problem?
options: A bounded rollout ring
A bounded model version
A raw user or device identifier on every metric point
A small hardware-family enum
questions.explanation: Per-user or per-device identifiers create large attribute combinations and can expose sensitive identity. Keep metric dimensions bounded and move detailed diagnostics to controlled logs or traces.

questions.question: What makes a rollback path credible?
options: The old model file exists somewhere in object storage
The previous model, runtime, feature schema, policy, and local cache were tested together
The new model has a larger version number
The rollout controller can restart a Pod
questions.explanation: Rollback restores a compatible system contract, not only bytes. Feature pipelines and runtime dependencies may have changed since the previous model was active.
